articles.title: Landed or condo: which holds its value better?
articles.excerpt: A reader assumes landed homes are guaranteed to appreciate while condos age. Sean explains why that view is hindsight, where condos win, and the price ceiling open landed homes run into.
articles.viewerQuestion: In a sought-after area such as Bukit Jalil, Hartamas or PJ, how would a condo's value hold up against a landed home over the long run?
articles.answer: Landed terrace houses do appreciate fastest, but "guaranteed" is hindsight. Condos in good locations grow a little more slowly yet earn far more rent, and older landed homes without security face a ceiling on what buyers will pay.
points: Landed wins on growth, condos win on rent
Yesterday's safe bet was once the fringe
Open landed homes hit a price ceiling
Big landed homes are hard to sell
questions: Do landed homes always appreciate more than condos?
Which is better for rental income: condo or landed?
Why do older landed homes without security have a price ceiling?
Are large landed homes hard to sell in Malaysia?
Should I buy a condo for rental yield or a landed home for capital growth?

articles.title: I cancelled my booking. Was it FOMO, or the right call?
articles.excerpt: A 25-year-old booked a RM640,000 unit on a promised 15% return, then cancelled. Sean explains why that was right, and how to tell what you can actually afford.
articles.viewerQuestion: Was walking away right, or too conservative? And how does he stop worrying that prices will run away before he is ready?
articles.answer: Cancelling was right. The numbers only worked if nothing went wrong, and on his income a property of around RM300,000 to RM400,000 is the safer place to start.
points: A 15% return is a red flag
Student-style buildings are hard to exit
He could not survive a bad year
Time yourself, not the market
questions: Did I make a mistake cancelling my property booking?
How much property can I afford on my income?
Is it safe to buy a property with a 15% promised return?
What should I check before paying a booking fee?

articles.title: When should you stop renting and buy a home?
articles.excerpt: A 34-year-old renter is tired of moving and wants a home of his own, but friends warn him off. Sean tests the decision with his 85% rule.
articles.viewerQuestion: Should he buy a home in the area he already lives in, or keep renting and invest the money instead?
articles.answer: Buy it. He can afford it, he knows the area, and the unit would rent for most of its instalment if his plans ever change. That is what makes an own-stay purchase safe.
points: It passes the 85% rule
He is buying where he already lives
His foundations are in place
A home pays you in certainty
questions: When should I stop renting and buy my own home?
How do I know if I can afford to buy a house?
What is the 85% rule for buying a home?
Should I buy a home in the area I already live in?
Is it better to buy a home or keep renting and invest?

articles.title: What should you check when you get your keys?
articles.excerpt: Most buyers hunt for scratches and hollow tiles and miss what stops a home from working. Sean sets out what to check first in a defect inspection.
articles.viewerQuestion: What should you check during a defect inspection, and in what order?
articles.answer: Check function before looks. Test every power point, water point, door and window first, compare the unit against your sale agreement, then move on to cosmetic flaws, and report everything through the proper channel.
points: Utilities come first
Water problems hide
Your sale agreement is the checklist
Hollow tiles are more serious than they look
questions: What should I check first during a defect inspection?
How do I test if tiles are hollow?
What should I bring for a defect inspection?
How long is the defect liability period?
Can I claim for leaks after moving in?

articles.title: I bought at a discount. Why am I still losing money?
articles.excerpt: A homeowner who bought "at a good rate" during COVID now struggles with the instalment and cannot find tenants. Sean explains why a discount is not a bargain, and how to decide whether to hold, rent or sell.
articles.viewerQuestion: Did he buy into a money-losing development, and what should he do now?
articles.answer: A discount only helps if the price ends up below the area's median, not just below the project's old price. For a home already bought, the question now is whether to hold, rent or sell, and that depends on valuation, recent sales and the loan balance.
points: The discount was measured against the wrong number
A quiet address does not draw tenants
The 85% test was never done
Who loses depends on when they bought

How do I know if my condo can cover its own instalment with rent?
Should I hold, rent out or sell my property that is not renting?
How do I check if my property is really worth what I paid?
Why can't I find tenants for my condo even at lower rent?

articles.title: Must your first property also be your home?
articles.excerpt: A 26-year-old bought an investment condo before a family home, and his future in-laws disapprove. Sean explains why investing first can be the smarter order.
articles.viewerQuestion: Is it better to buy a home first and invest later? And how should he explain his plan to in-laws who think he is being too aggressive?
articles.answer: Invest first and keep renting your home. Use your strongest borrowing years and your cheapest loans on property that tenants help pay for, and buy the family home later.
points: The 90% loans are worth using early
A home tends to become a big commitment
Judge it over 20 years, not in month one
Renting keeps the couple flexible

How do I explain to my in-laws that renting and investing is a good plan?
What are the benefits of using a 90% loan for an investment property?
How long should I wait before buying my next investment property?
Should a young couple rent their home and invest first?

articles.title: Is a guaranteed rental return worth buying into?
articles.excerpt: A reader has booked a hotel unit with a guaranteed 7% return. Sean explains where the guarantee really comes from, and why the exit is the bigger problem.
articles.viewerQuestion: He worries about the narrow access road, the operator choosing not to renew after nine years, and another pandemic. Is this kind of investment worth it?
articles.answer: Stay away unless it is a third or fourth property you can afford to lose. The guaranteed return is your own borrowed money paid back to you, the price is inflated, and the hotel operator is your only way out.
points: The guarantee is built into the price
You are paying city-centre prices for Genting
There is only one way out
The real return is thinner than 7%

articles.title: What does buying a property really cost beyond the 10%?
articles.excerpt: Most first-time buyers budget the deposit and nothing else. Sean lists the costs that kept surprising him on his first purchase.
articles.viewerQuestion: What else do you actually have to pay when you buy a property?
articles.answer: Budget well beyond the deposit. Legal fees on both the purchase and the loan, transfer stamp duty, valuation, handover deposits, compulsory insurance and yearly taxes all fall on the buyer, and a subsale costs the most upfront.
points: Legal fees come with more than one agreement
The transfer duty is the big one
Handover comes with deposits
Some costs never stop

articles.title: I'm over 60. Should I still invest in property?
articles.excerpt: A reader over 60 is being offered short-stay units promising 9% returns. Sean explains why property loses its main advantage at that age, and what to consider instead.
articles.viewerQuestion: Should she invest in property at her age? Should she pay cash or borrow, buy new or subsale, and are these short-stay projects worth it?
articles.answer: Probably not as a main plan. Property's big advantage is decades of cheap borrowing that tenants help repay, and at 60 that is mostly gone. Low-risk options paying a similar return, without the hassle or locked-up money, suit her better.
points: The leverage advantage is mostly gone
Property locks your money up
Other assets pay similar returns more easily
Advertised short-stay returns rarely last

articles.title: Is "location, location, location" still the rule?
articles.excerpt: A young investor has shortlisted Bangsar South by its rental demand. Sean argues that location is not what makes you money; the price you pay against the area median is.
articles.viewerQuestion: Is "location, location, location" still the rule? Should he pay more for a newer project or buy an older subsale, and could he fund it with a 36-month interest-free credit card plan?
articles.answer: Location matters less than people think. Most KL areas will end up with the same amenities, so your profit is decided by your entry price: buy below the area's median price.
points: Entry price decides profit, not the postcode
High rent follows temporary demand
New costs more but ages better
A subsale starts earning sooner

articles.title: A baby is coming. Move in, or rent out our first home?
articles.excerpt: A couple bought a new condo as their first home, but their first child arrives as it is handed over. Sean explains why he would rent it out and stay with family for now.
articles.viewerQuestion: With a baby coming, should they stay with his parents, rent the unit out and live elsewhere, or move in as planned despite the renovation noise from 1,300 new neighbours?
articles.answer: Stay with family for the first year or two and rent River Park out from handover. Treat it as an investment, and move somewhere that suits the baby later, renting if you need to.
points: A newborn needs hands more than space
The unit works better as a rental
1,300 new units is less of a threat than it looks
Moving in now means a year of drilling

articles.title: Should you buy new from a developer or a subsale?
articles.excerpt: A new launch and a subsale unit can cost the same on paper but ask for very different cash, time and risk. Sean explains who each one suits.
articles.viewerQuestion: Should you buy new from a developer, or a subsale unit?
articles.answer: It depends on your cash and experience. Investors with capital should favour a subsale, where you can see the real condition and rent from day one. First-time buyers short on cash are better served by a new launch.
points: A new launch needs far less cash upfront
Developers handle the paperwork
With a subsale, what you see is what you get
A subsale earns rent straight away

articles.title: Cheap old house or new house with no down payment?
articles.excerpt: An unmarried couple must choose between a cheap 30-year-old house needing renovation and a new one with a bigger instalment. Sean says the real question is whose income the loan depends on.
articles.viewerQuestion: Should they spend most of their savings on the old house with the easy instalment, or take the new house with little cash upfront but double the monthly commitment?
articles.answer: Take the old house, and buy it in one name. On one income, a RM3,000 instalment is out of reach, and counting on a partner who has not committed to living in Seremban is the real risk.
points: Do not borrow on income you cannot count on
Compare with the area median, not the new house
Renovation does not add its cost to the value
An old house is as good as how it was lived in

articles.title: My parents will pay half. Must I buy a home to live in?
articles.excerpt: A first-time investor's parents will pay half the price, but only for a home to live in. Sean explains how to protect a one-income household and handle the condition.
articles.viewerQuestion: Is her money enough, or too risky while her husband's business is unstable? Should she buy new or subsale, and how should she handle her parents' condition?
articles.answer: Protect your savings while the household runs on one income, and accept your parents' help graciously. Buy through a channel that needs little cash, and if the condition is a home, choose one that would still rent well.

Subsale and auction need too much cash
New launches and bulk deals need the least cash
Half the price is generous, with strings

articles.title: How do you know a project is not overpriced?
articles.excerpt: Projects borrow the name of a famous neighbourhood to charge its prices. Sean walks through the research that shows what an address is really worth.
articles.viewerQuestion: What research do you need to do to know whether a project is priced right?
articles.answer: Go beyond the listing. Work out where the real neighbourhood ends, which tier of tenant it attracts, and compare the project only against like-for-like transacted prices: new against new, old against old, in the same tier.
points: A borrowed name does not bring borrowed rents
Know which tier you are buying into
Compare new with new and old with old
Make sure two rental plans break even

articles.title: Should I buy a second property, or keep it simple?
articles.excerpt: A 32-year-old government officer already owns a Klang Valley unit and invests in global equities. He asks whether two new projects with rebates are really good deals, or just sales tactics.
articles.viewerQuestion: Are these genuinely good investments or do the rebates make the numbers look better than they are, and with equities already in place, is another leveraged property worthwhile?
articles.answer: The rebates are retail-price sales tactics that everybody gets, and a newer project only wins when the entry price makes sense. Let the existing unit run, use your second 90% loan slot only when you can afford it, and keep the capital a third property would need in global equities.
points: Newer wins only if the price makes sense
Rebates are given to everybody
The exit depends on rent, not age
Cash in property is the worst deal

articles.title: Should You Settle Your Housing Loan Early?
articles.excerpt: A reader with three mortgages dreams of being debt-free. Sean explains why he would keep the loans running, and what to do with the spare cash instead.
articles.viewerQuestion: Should she pay the loans off as fast as possible to save on interest, or let them run the full term?
articles.answer: Keep the loans running. At around 4%, a housing loan is the cheapest money you can get, below the rate of inflation, so spare cash should go where it earns more than the loan costs.

Your cash can earn more elsewhere
Her loans already pay for themselves
Her age favours more borrowing, not less

articles.title: My project has stalled. Will it be abandoned?
articles.excerpt: A buyer sees construction slowing and fears the project will be abandoned. Sean, a buyer in the same project, explains the difference between ailing and abandoned, and the real options for getting out or staying in.
articles.viewerQuestion: Is the project in trouble, and what can a buyer actually do if it ends up abandoned?
articles.answer: An ailing project is not an abandoned one. Check its official status, then choose between staying in for delay compensation or walking away at a cost. A full refund is very hard to get.

The developer is selling assets to fix it
Walking away costs money; a full refund is rare
Staying in can still pay off

articles.title: Is it a good time to buy? What ten years of data says
articles.excerpt: Why did some Malaysians lose money on property over the past decade? Sean reads ten years of official data and swaps timing for a test you can actually apply.
articles.viewerQuestion: Why did some buyers lose money over the last decade, and how do you tell whether it is a good time to buy?
articles.answer: Nobody can time the market, so stop trying. If your finances are ready, buy only below the location's past transacted median, with rent that gives a healthy yield. That limits the damage even if you happen to buy at a peak.
points: When you bought decided who lost
Property does not double every ten years
Nobody can call the bottom
The outlook is positive, but supply is rising
